paragraphs.source_en: The ethnographic record that is particularly suitable for the interpretation of the Round Head paintings seems to be that of Southern Africa. In southern African rock art studies ethnographic materials have built a model which focuses on trance and shamanic visions (Solomon 1998). Even though it cannot be applied directly to the central Saharan rock art, there are some striking similarities in the painted scenes of the two regions which suggest that a possible similar ideology persisted in time and space. The most significant common points, regarding mainly the rain-making sphere, are presented later.

paragraphs.source_en: Also the results of rock art research in other regions, although they may have very ancient common roots, cannot be applied directly to the Saharan paintings, and they must be considered as a guide only, which may lead to a possible interpretation. The similarities between various artistic traditions remain indicative, since apparently the same scenes in various regions may have had a different meaning in their times. In this chapter I examine the features of the Round Head paintings which I consider significant for the interpretation of this art. I combine the information from the paintings with those of the excavations and the landscape, and I use the ethnographic records from several African regions of people producing rock art, as well as those who do not produce it.
